meta.name: Smoke Inhalation — Early Intubation Before Airway Closure

patient.name: Marcus Delaney
patient.chiefComplaint: Difficulty breathing and hoarse voice after house fire

history.hpi: Patient was inside a single-family home when a kitchen fire spread rapidly; he was trapped in a smoke-filled hallway for an estimated 5-8 minutes before self-extricating out a rear door. Reports his voice "feels tight" and swallowing is uncomfortable. Denies loss of consciousness. Firefighters on scene report heavy black smoke with synthetic furniture and carpet involved.
history.lastOralIntake: Dinner approximately 2 hours prior to the fire
history.events: Neighbors called 911 after seeing smoke; patient self-extricated and was found sitting on the curb by first-arriving engine company

scene.dispatch: 40-year-old male, structure fire, patient out of the building, difficulty breathing
scene.location: Residential street, patient seated on curb approximately 30 feet from a single-family home with heavy smoke showing from the roofline
scene.safety: Active structure fire with fire suppression in progress; scene secured by fire command outside the hot zone; patient already extricated
scene.bystanders: Neighbor who called 911 present; reports patient was inside for several minutes before getting out on his own
visualCues: Soot around the nares and mouth
Mild inspiratory stridor audible without a stethoscope
Heavy smoke and fire activity visible in the background

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew finds a 40-year-old male seated on the curb, anxious and coughing, with visible soot around his nose and mouth and a hoarse voice. He self-extricated from a smoke-filled structure fire minutes ago.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent but hoarse voice, soot around nares/mouth, singed nasal hairs, mild audible inspiratory stridor
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Tachypneic, mild accessory muscle use, occasional cough productive of carbonaceous sputum
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present bilaterally, strong and rapid, skin warm and diaphoretic
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "My throat feels really tight... it's getting harder to talk."

transitions.condition: Crew places the patient on 100% oxygen and attaches cardiac monitor, pulse oximetry, and capnography while obtaining a focused exposure history.

phases.name: High-flow O2 and monitoring started
phases.description: Patient placed on 100% oxygen via non-rebreather with continuous monitoring. The crew recognizes that pulse oximetry may be falsely reassuring given probable carbon monoxide exposure, and continues serial airway reassessment given the risk of progressive swelling.
phases.triggerCondition: After removal from the toxic environment, the crew immediately initiates 100% oxygen and full monitoring per the Carbon Monoxide/Smoke Inhalation guideline, understanding that pulse oximetry does not reliably reflect tissue oxygenation in this setting.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Hoarseness worsening compared to initial contact, stridor slightly more pronounced
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Tachypneic, 100% oxygen via non-rebreather in place
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present, strong and rapid
otherFindings: Voice noticeably more hoarse than 2 minutes ago

expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: 100% oxygen via non-rebreather mask or high flow oxygen by nasal cannula (HFNC) or CPAP or bag valve mask or advanced airway as indicated
expectedActions.rationale: Carbon monoxide has high affinity for hemoglobin; high-flow oxygen accelerates its displacement even when pulse oximetry appears normal.

expectedActions.shortAction: Apply cardiac monitor, pulse oximetry, and EtCO2; check blood glucose
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Vital signs (pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, neurologic status assessment) temperature, and O2 saturation, and EtCO2 if available. Apply a cardiac monitor, examine rhythm strip for arrhythmias, and obtain a 12-lead EKG if available. Check blood glucose level
expectedActions.rationale: Establishes baseline monitoring and rules out other contributing causes of altered vitals.

expectedActions.shortAction: Do not rely on normal SpO2 to exclude significant CO or cyanide toxicity
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Pulse oximetry is inaccurate due to the carbon monoxide binding with hemoglobin
expectedActions.rationale: A reassuring SpO2 can mask severe hypoxic injury from CO/cyanide binding rather than true oxygen desaturation.

transitions.if: Early RSI performed for impending obstruction
transitions.condition: Worsening hoarseness, increasing stridor, and visible soot/carbonaceous sputum in the oropharynx are recognized as signs of impending airway obstruction, prompting early RSI before the airway swells shut.
Crew defers airway management, waiting for further deterioration instead of intubating early; stridor and hoarseness progress toward near-complete obstruction.
Patient develops sudden hypotension and worsening mental status out of proportion to visible burn severity, raising concern for concurrent cyanide toxicity from combustion of synthetic materials.

phases.name: Early RSI performed for impending obstruction
phases.description: Recognizing progressive hoarseness, stridor, and airway soot as signs of impending obstruction from inhalation injury, the crew performs RSI before the airway swells further, securing a definitive airway while it is still possible to visualize the cords.
phases.triggerCondition: Worsening hoarseness, increasing inspiratory stridor, and visible airway soiling are recognized as an evolving inhalation injury with impending airway obstruction, meeting the protocol's indication for early intubation before complete closure occurs.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Marked hoarseness, audible stridor, oropharynx visibly sooty; preparing for RSI while cords still visualizable
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present, strong and rapid
otherFindings: Two experienced airway practitioners at bedside

expectedActions.shortAction: Preoxygenate with high-flow O2 and positive pressure for 2 minutes before RSI
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patient should be pre-oxygenated with high flow oxygen, and positive pressure ventilation for a minimum of two minutes prior to the procedure
expectedActions.rationale: Maximizes oxygen reserve before apnea during induction and paralysis.

expectedActions.shortAction: Suction soot/secretions from oropharynx before laryngoscopy
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Prompt suctioning of soiled airways before intubation attempt may improve first pass success and limit morbidity and mortality
expectedActions.rationale: Carbonaceous debris in the airway can obscure the glottic view and increase aspiration risk.

expectedActions.shortAction: Fentanyl 90 mcg IV premedication (90 kg × 1 mcg/kg), 2-3 min before intubation
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Consider pre-medication with Fentanyl, 1 mcg/kg, 2-3 minutes prior to intubation attempt
expectedActions.rationale: Blunts the sympathetic response to laryngoscopy.

expectedActions.shortAction: Etomidate 27 mg IV push (90 kg × 0.3 mg/kg)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Administer induction sedative agent: Etomidate IV push, 0.2-0.3 mg/kg
expectedActions.rationale: Provides rapid sedation with minimal hemodynamic effect prior to paralysis.

expectedActions.shortAction: Rocuronium 90 mg IV push (90 kg × 1 mg/kg)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Administer paralytic agent: Rocuronium IV push, 1 mg/kg
expectedActions.rationale: Achieves complete paralysis for optimal first-pass intubation conditions.

expectedActions.shortAction: Intubate with 8.0 mm ETT (adult male), limit attempt to 15 seconds or SpO2 <90%
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Absent significant airway swelling or underlying anatomic abnormalities, initial tube size (internal diameter in millimeters) for adult females should be 7.5, adult males 8.0. Attempt intubation, limiting attempts to 15 seconds, or a desaturation below 90%, whichever occurs first
expectedActions.rationale: Secures the airway before further swelling makes glottic visualization impossible.

transitions.condition: Successful first-pass intubation is confirmed with waveform capnography, bilateral breath sounds, and absent gastric sounds; tube is secured and ventilation begins.

phases.name: Tube confirmed and secured, transport initiated
phases.description: The endotracheal tube is confirmed with waveform capnography, secured, and the patient is ventilated and transported. Given the severity of exposure, the crew considers a facility with hyperbaric oxygen capability.
phases.triggerCondition: After successful intubation, tube placement is confirmed and secured, and the patient is transported with continuous capnography monitoring.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Secured with endotracheal tube, confirmed placement, bilateral breath sounds equal
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial and pedal pulses present, skin warm
otherFindings: ETT secured at appropriate depth, tube position reassessed after each movement
Considering hyperbaric-capable facility given severity of exposure

expectedActions.shortAction: Confirm tube placement with waveform capnography, secure tube, reassess after each movement
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Confirm placement of advanced airway (endotracheal tube, SGA) with waveform capnography (most reliable), absent gastric sounds, and bilateral breath sounds. Secure tube manually. Once proper position is confirmed, secure the tube with tape, twill, or commercial device
expectedActions.rationale: Waveform capnography is the most reliable confirmation method and must be continuously monitored for displacement.

expectedActions.shortAction: Consider direct transport to a hyperbaric-capable facility given severe CO exposure
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Consider transporting patients with severe carbon monoxide poisoning directly to a facility with hyperbaric oxygen capabilities if feasible and patient does not meet criteria for other specialty care (e.g., trauma or burn)
expectedActions.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy reduces the risk of delayed neurologic sequelae from significant CO exposure.

phases.name: Intubation delayed despite worsening stridor
phases.description: The crew waits for further deterioration instead of intubating while the airway is still manageable. Stridor becomes severe, the glottic opening becomes difficult to visualize due to progressive swelling, and oxygenation begins to fail.
phases.triggerCondition: Airway management is deferred despite worsening hoarseness and stridor; progressive edema narrows the airway to the point that intubation becomes difficult or impossible, and a surgical airway may be required.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Severe stridor, minimal air movement, oropharyngeal swelling now obscures the glottic opening
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Marked accessory muscle use, paradoxical chest movement, weak respiratory effort
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present but thready, tachycardic
otherFindings: Unable to speak now, only whispering
Glottic structures no longer clearly visualized on attempted laryngoscopy

expectedActions.shortAction: Prepare for surgical airway; oxygenation/ventilation cannot be achieved by less invasive means
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: When patients cannot be oxygenated/ventilated effectively using the above interventions, or when conventional airway approaches are impossible, surgical airway management is a reasonable option if the clinician has competency in the procedure and risk of death for not escalating airway management seems to outweigh the risk of a procedural complication
expectedActions.rationale: Delayed recognition of impending obstruction can progress to a can't-intubate, can't-oxygenate emergency requiring surgical airway rescue.

phases.name: Hydroxocobalamin given for suspected cyanide toxicity
phases.description: The patient develops sudden hypotension and worsening mental status disproportionate to the visible burn severity. Given the fire involved synthetic materials, concurrent cyanide toxicity is suspected and empiric treatment is initiated.
phases.triggerCondition: Sudden hypotension and rapidly worsening mental status, out of proportion to visible injury, in a patient exposed to combustion of synthetic materials raises concern for concurrent cyanide toxicity requiring empiric antidote treatment.

otherFindings: Rapid decline in mental status disproportionate to apparent burn severity
Hypotension not explained by visible blood loss
Fire involved significant synthetic furniture/carpet combustion per fire crew report

expectedActions.shortAction: Hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV over 15 minutes for suspected cyanide toxicity
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Administer hydroxocobalamin: Initial dose is 5 g administered over 15 minutes slow IV. Each 5 g vial of hydroxocobalamin for injection is to be reconstituted with 200 mL of LR, NS, or D5W (25 mg/mL) and administered at 10-15 mL/minute
expectedActions.rationale: Fire smoke from synthetic materials can generate cyanide; treatment decisions are made clinically since rapid confirmatory testing is unavailable.

expectedActions.shortAction: Continue 100% oxygen via non-rebreather, CPAP, or BVM as tolerated
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: 100% oxygen via non-rebreather mask, CPAP, or bag valve mask
expectedActions.rationale: High-flow oxygen remains essential supportive therapy alongside antidote administration.
